hints: Focus on what actually happens when a liquid boils, the forces between molecules breaking, not the bonds inside molecules.
Compare oxygen and sulfur for electronegativity and size, and recall the two strict conditions needed for hydrogen bonding.
Link the much stronger intermolecular attraction in one of these molecules to the extra energy needed to separate its molecules into a gas.
walkthrough:
**What boiling really breaks**

Boiling separates molecules from each other. It overcomes intermolecular forces, it does not break strong covalent bonds inside the molecules.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{boiling breaks intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds}$$

**Why water is special**

Oxygen is small and very electronegative, so in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ we get $\text{O}^{\delta-}$ and $\text{H}^{\delta+}$. This allows strong hydrogen bonds between molecules: $\text{O-H} \cdots \text{O}$.

Attraction:
$$\text{H}^{\delta+} \cdots \text{O}^{\delta-} \text{ hydrogen bond}$$

**Why H2S cannot do the same**

Sulfur is larger and much less electronegative than oxygen. So $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ has only weaker permanent dipole-dipole forces and induced dipole forces, with no significant hydrogen bonding.

Conclusion:
$$\text{stronger intermolecular forces in H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{more energy needed} \rightarrow \text{higher boiling point}$$

options.A: O-H is indeed stronger than S-H, but this is intramolecular covalent bond energy. Boiling does not break O-H or S-H covalent bonds, so this cannot explain the boiling point difference.
options.B: This is backwards. If forces in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ were weaker, water would boil more easily and have a lower boiling point. In fact the forces in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ are much stronger.
options.C: The S-H bond is longer than O-H because sulfur is a larger atom, and this statement is true. However bond length is an intramolecular property and does not control how strongly separate molecules attract each other.
options.D: This is correct and complete. $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ meets the conditions for hydrogen bonding (H attached to small, highly electronegative O with lone pairs), while $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ does not. The extra strong hydrogen bonds need much more energy to break, giving water the higher boiling point.
